source: CD133 (prominin 1) is widely viewed as a cancer stem cell marker in association with drug resistance and cancer recurrence.

claim: With impaired RTK-Shp2-Ras-Erk signaling, heterogenous hepatocytes form clusters that manage to divide during mouse liver regeneration.

source: These hepatocytes are characterized by upregulated CD133 while negative for other progenitor cell markers.

claim: Pharmaceutical inhibition of proliferative signaling induced CD133 expression in various cancer cell types from multiple animal species.

claim: Liver regeneration is a widely used animal model to dissect mechanisms that drive cell proliferation in vivo.

claim: The unique regenerative capacity of the liver is conserved from animals to humans.
source: Liver regeneration is a widely used animal model to dissect mechanisms that drive cell proliferation in vivo, with the unique regenerative capacity conserved from animals to humans (Fausto et al., 2006; Michalopoulos and DeFrances, 1997; Taub, 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by cited references.

claim: Partial hepatectomy (PHx) of two-thirds liver in rodents is a frequently used experimental platform for studying liver regeneration.
source: One frequently used experimental platform is partial hepatectomy (PHx) of two-thirds liver in rodents.

claim: Re-entering the cell cycle of quiescent hepatocytes in the adult liver is believed to be a primary mechanism of liver regeneration.
source: Although re-entering the cell cycle of quiescent hepatocytes in the adult liver is believed to be a primary mechanism of liver regeneration, the possible involvement of stem/progenitor cells has also been explored (Michalopoulos, 2017; Miyajima et al., 2014).

claim: The possible involvement of stem/progenitor cells in liver regeneration has been explored.

claim: Conflicting data exist regarding the source and contribution of putative stem/progenitor cells in liver regeneration and hepato-carcinogenesis following hepatic injuries.

claim: A CD133+ cell population was regarded as a source of progenitor cells that contribute to liver regeneration.

claim: A rapid increase of growth factors in the liver and blood, including HGF, EGF, IL-6, and TNFα, is detected immediately following PHx.
source: Detected immediately following PHx was a rapid increase of growth factors in the liver and blood, including HGF, EGF, IL-6, and TNFα (Michalopoulos, 2017), accompanied by upregulation of proliferative signaling events, especially the Ras-Erk pathway, in hepatocytes.

claim: The rapid increase of growth factors following PHx is accompanied by upregulation of proliferative signaling events, especially the Ras-Erk pathway, in hepatocytes.
source: Detected immediately following PHx was a rapid increase of growth factors in the liver and blood, including HGF, EGF, IL-6, and TNFα (Michalopoulos, 2017), accompanied by upregulation of proliferative signaling events, especially the Ras-Erk pathway, in hepatocytes.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by a citation.

claim: Shp2/Ptpn11 is an SH2-containing tyrosine phosphatase.
source: Shp2/Ptpn11, an SH2-containing tyrosine phosphatase, is a key molecule that promotes signaling from receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs) to the Ras-Erk pathway (Chan and Feng, 2007; Chen et al., 2016; Grossmann et al., 2010; Matozaki et al., 2009; Tajan et al., 2015).

claim: Shp2 is a key molecule that promotes signaling from receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs) to the Ras-Erk pathway.
source: Shp2/Ptpn11, an SH2-containing tyrosine phosphatase, is a key molecule that promotes signaling from receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs) to the Ras-Erk pathway (Chan and Feng, 2007; Chen et al., 2016; Grossmann et al., 2010; Matozaki et al., 2009; Tajan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Ablating Shp2 in hepatocytes attenuated hepatocyte proliferation following PHx.
source: Ablating Shp2 in hepatocytes attenuated hepatocyte proliferation following PHx and also suppressed RTK-driven hepato-oncogenesis (Bard-Chapeau et al., 2006; Chen et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is prior work from the authors' group, supported by citations.

claim: Ablating Shp2 in hepatocytes suppressed RTK-driven hepato-oncogenesis.
source: Ablating Shp2 in hepatocytes attenuated hepatocyte proliferation following PHx and also suppressed RTK-driven hepato-oncogenesis (Bard-Chapeau et al., 2006; Chen et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is prior work from the authors' group, supported by citations.

claim: Liver regeneration was impaired but not blocked by the removal of Shp2 or other pro-proliferative molecules in hepatocytes.
source: Of note, liver regeneration was impaired but not blocked by the removal of Shp2 or other pro-proliferative molecules in hepatocytes (Fausto et al., 2006; Michalopoulos and DeFrances, 1997; Taub, 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: A critical question is why and how a small number of hepatocytes overcome the diminished mitogenic signaling to re-gain proliferative capacity.
source: Thus, one critical question is why and how a small number of hepatocytes overcome the diminished mitogenic signaling, to re-gain proliferative capacity.
evidence: This is the research question that motivates the study.

claim: In Shp2-deficient livers, actively dividing hepatocytes formed distinctive clusters.
source: In this study, we found that in Shp2-deficient livers, actively dividing hepatocytes formed distinctive clusters and highly expressed CD133, but were negative for other stem/progenitor cell markers.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study.

claim: Actively dividing hepatocytes in Shp2-deficient livers highly expressed CD133 but were negative for other stem/progenitor cell markers.
source: In this study, we found that in Shp2-deficient livers, actively dividing hepatocytes formed distinctive clusters and highly expressed CD133, but were negative for other stem/progenitor cell markers.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study.

claim: The CD133+ cell colonies appeared transiently following PHx and disappeared quickly after the completion of liver regeneration.
source: The CD133+ cell colonies appeared transiently following PHx and disappeared quickly after the completion of liver regeneration.
evidence: This is a finding from time-course experiments in the study.

claim: CD133+ cell colonies were observed in MET-deficient livers following liver injuries.
source: This phenotype was also observed in MET-deficient livers following liver injuries.
evidence: This is a finding from experiments with MET-deficient mice.

claim: CD133 expression was upregulated by proliferative signal inhibition in a variety of cancer cell lines from different organs.
source: CD133 expression was upregulated by proliferative signal inhibition in a variety of cancer cell lines from different organs, indicating a commonly shared mechanism.
evidence: This is a finding from experiments with multiple cancer cell lines.

claim: CD133 upregulation by proliferative signal inhibition indicates a commonly shared mechanism.
source: CD133 expression was upregulated by proliferative signal inhibition in a variety of cancer cell lines from different organs, indicating a commonly shared mechanism.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings across multiple cell types.

claim: CD133+ intracellular vesicles are enriched with transcripts of immediate early responsive genes (IEGs).
source: Remarkably, we identified and isolated CD133+ intracellular vesicles, which were enriched with transcripts of immediate early responsive genes (IEGs) and migrated between tightly contacting cells in colonies.
evidence: This is a finding from RNA analysis of isolated CD133+ vesicles.

claim: CD133+ intracellular vesicles migrated between tightly contacting cells in colonies.
source: Remarkably, we identified and isolated CD133+ intracellular vesicles, which were enriched with transcripts of immediate early responsive genes (IEGs) and migrated between tightly contacting cells in colonies.
evidence: This is a finding from microscopy observations.

claim: Cells defective for proliferative signaling exhibited lower intracellular transcriptional diversity (entropy).
source: Single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) demonstrated that cells defective for proliferative signaling exhibited lower intracellular transcriptional diversity (entropy), which was remedied in CD133+ cells, potentially by converting intercellular heterogeneity into intracellular diversity through sharing of mRNAs.
evidence: This is a finding from scRNA-seq analysis.

claim: Lower intracellular transcriptional diversity in cells defective for proliferative signaling was remedied in CD133+ cells.
source: Single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) demonstrated that cells defective for proliferative signaling exhibited lower intracellular transcriptional diversity (entropy), which was remedied in CD133+ cells, potentially by converting intercellular heterogeneity into intracellular diversity through sharing of mRNAs.
evidence: This is a finding from scRNA-seq analysis.

claim: CD133+ cells potentially convert intercellular heterogeneity into intracellular diversity through sharing of mRNAs.
source: Single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) demonstrated that cells defective for proliferative signaling exhibited lower intracellular transcriptional diversity (entropy), which was remedied in CD133+ cells, potentially by converting intercellular heterogeneity into intracellular diversity through sharing of mRNAs.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on scRNA-seq data and mathematical modeling.

claim: The data suggest a new function of CD133 in intercellular communication.
source: These data suggest a new function of CD133 in intercellular communication, by which normal and cancer cells endeavor to proliferate under proliferative signal deficit.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the collective findings.

claim: Normal and cancer cells endeavor to proliferate under proliferative signal deficit through CD133-mediated intercellular communication.
source: These data suggest a new function of CD133 in intercellular communication, by which normal and cancer cells endeavor to proliferate under proliferative signal deficit.

claim: At 2 days after PHx, WT and SKO livers exhibited similar overall and histological phenotypes.
source: At 2 days after PHx, WT and SKO livers exhibited similar overall and histological phenotypes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is an observation from histological analysis, with reference to supplementary figures.

claim: Immunostaining for Ki67 showed significantly lower numbers of proliferating hepatocytes in SKO than WT livers.
source: Immunostaining for Ki67 showed significantly lower numbers of proliferating hepatocytes in SKO than WT livers, with no difference for non-parenchymal cells (NPCs) where Shp2 was not deleted (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, and 1D).
evidence: This is a finding from immunostaining experiments, with reference to figures.

claim: There was no difference in proliferating non-parenchymal cells (NPCs) between SKO and WT livers where Shp2 was not deleted.
source: Immunostaining for Ki67 showed significantly lower numbers of proliferating hepatocytes in SKO than WT livers, with no difference for non-parenchymal cells (NPCs) where Shp2 was not deleted (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, and 1D).
evidence: This is a finding from immunostaining experiments, with reference to figures.

claim: Certain areas in SKO liver were enriched with proliferating hepatocytes.
source: Intriguingly, we identified certain areas that were enriched with proliferating hepatocytes in SKO liver (Figure 1A; arrow).
evidence: This is an observation from immunostaining, with reference to a figure.

claim: Areas enriched with proliferating hepatocytes in SKO liver did not display severe inflammation or different phenotypes of hepatocytes except active proliferation.
source: This peculiar proliferation pattern was especially cryptic, because these areas did not display severe inflammation or different phenotypes of hepatocytes except active proliferation (Figure 1A; right panel).
evidence: This is an observation from histological analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: CD133 was the only molecule that was highly expressed in the areas enriched with proliferating hepatocytes among the biomarkers tested.
source: Therefore, we searched extensively for biomarker molecules, which could distinguish the actively proliferating cells in the particular areas, including GFAP, EpCAM, CK19, CD133, Sox9, CD44, and α-fetoprotein (AFP) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–1H). Of note, CD133 was the only molecule that was highly expressed in the areas enriched with proliferating hepatocytes (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from screening multiple biomarkers, with reference to figures.

claim: The percentages of Ki67+ hepatocytes were significantly higher in CD133+ than in CD133− areas in regenerating livers.
source: The percentages of Ki67+ hepatocytes were significantly higher in CD133+ than in CD133− areas in regenerating livers (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from immunostaining analysis, with reference to figures.

claim: Patchy areas with CD133+ hepatocytes appeared 2 days after PHx and underwent expansion until 3 weeks.
source: These patchy areas appeared 2 days after PHx, and underwent expansion until 3 weeks, whereas WT livers did not show comparable CD133 expression in hepatocytes (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a finding from time-course experiments, with reference to a figure.

claim: WT livers did not show comparable CD133 expression in hepatocytes after PHx.
source: These patchy areas appeared 2 days after PHx, and underwent expansion until 3 weeks, whereas WT livers did not show comparable CD133 expression in hepatocytes (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a finding from immunostaining experiments, with reference to a figure.

claim: Liver/body weight ratios were similar between SKO and WT mice by 3 weeks after PHx.
source: Liver/body weight ratios were similar between SKO and WT mice by 3 weeks (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I), suggesting that the active division of CD133+ cells could compensate for the impaired proliferative capacity of CD133− hepatocytes in SKO liver.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experiments, with reference to a figure.

claim: The active division of CD133+ cells could compensate for the impaired proliferative capacity of CD133− hepatocytes in SKO liver.
source: Liver/body weight ratios were similar between SKO and WT mice by 3 weeks (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I), suggesting that the active division of CD133+ cells could compensate for the impaired proliferative capacity of CD133− hepatocytes in SKO liver.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the liver/body weight ratio data.

claim: CD133+ hepatocytes expressed high levels of E-cadherin and displayed tight cell-cell contact in the colonies.
source: The CD133+ hepatocytes also expressed high levels of E-cadherin and displayed tight cell-cell contact in the colonies (Figure 2A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1J and K).
evidence: This is a finding from immunostaining experiments, with reference to figures.

claim: CD133 was localized to the apical side of hepatocytes.
source: CD133 was localized to the apical side of hepatocytes (Figure 2A), and was rarely detected in other types of cells located on their basal sides.
evidence: This is a finding from immunostaining experiments, with reference to a figure.

claim: CD133 was rarely detected in other types of cells located on the basal sides of hepatocytes.
source: CD133 was localized to the apical side of hepatocytes (Figure 2A), and was rarely detected in other types of cells located on their basal sides.
evidence: This is a finding from immunostaining experiments, with reference to a figure.

claim: At 3 weeks after PHx, the colonies appeared more distinctive even in H&E staining and contained smaller hepatocytes with compact structure.
source: At 3 weeks after PHx, the colonies appeared more distinctive even in H&E staining, which contained smaller hepatocytes with compact structure, albeit no difference observed for NPC types and the vasculature (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a finding from histological analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: At 3 weeks after PHx, no difference was observed for NPC types and the vasculature in the colonies.
source: At 3 weeks after PHx, the colonies appeared more distinctive even in H&E staining, which contained smaller hepatocytes with compact structure, albeit no difference observed for NPC types and the vasculature (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a finding from histological analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: Immunostaining for sinusoidal endothelial cells and HGF did not show any unique features in the colonies.
source: Immunostaining for sinusoidal endothelial cells and HGF did not show any unique features in the colonies otherwise (Figure 1—figure supplement 1L and M).
evidence: This is a finding from immunostaining experiments, with reference to figures.

claim: The distinct colonies merged into surrounding tissues 5 weeks after PHx, as evidenced by loss of CD133 expression and disappearance of clear colony edges.
source: The distinct colonies merged into surrounding tissues 5 weeks after PHx, as evidenced by loss of CD133 expression and disappearance of clear colony edges (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a finding from time-course experiments, with reference to a figure.

claim: The CD133+ colonies of proliferating hepatocytes were composed transiently during liver regeneration.
source: Therefore, the CD133+ colonies of proliferating hepatocytes were composed transiently during liver regeneration.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the time-course observations.

claim: A clear difference in light scattering/refraction was observed in unstained thick liver sections due to the compacting colony architecture 3 weeks after PHx.
source: Due to the compacting colony architecture 3 weeks after PHx, we observed a clear difference in light scattering/refraction in unstained thick liver sections (Figure 2D), which allowed manual dissection of the colonies out of liver sections for analysis.
evidence: This is an observation from examining unstained tissue sections, with reference to a figure.

claim: The difference in light scattering/refraction allowed manual dissection of the colonies out of liver sections for analysis.
source: Due to the compacting colony architecture 3 weeks after PHx, we observed a clear difference in light scattering/refraction in unstained thick liver sections (Figure 2D), which allowed manual dissection of the colonies out of liver sections for analysis.
evidence: This is a methodological observation, with reference to a figure.

claim: Immunoblotting confirmed the enrichment of CD133+ and E-cadherin+ cells in the isolated colonies.
source: Immunoblotting confirmed the enrichment of CD133+ and E-cadherin+ cells but barely detected Shp2 protein in the isolated colonies, indicating their origin from Shp2-deleted hepatocytes (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: This is a finding from immunoblotting experiments, with reference to figures.

claim: Shp2 protein was barely detected in the isolated colonies, indicating their origin from Shp2-deleted hepatocytes.
source: Immunoblotting confirmed the enrichment of CD133+ and E-cadherin+ cells but barely detected Shp2 protein in the isolated colonies, indicating their origin from Shp2-deleted hepatocytes (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: This is a finding from immunoblotting experiments and its interpretation, with reference to figures.

claim: The expression of other oval cell markers, including EpCAM, AFP, and Sox9, was not observed in the colony lysates.
source: CD133 is known to be expressed in oval cells, which can differentiate into both hepatocytes and bile duct epithelial cells, similar to the potential of hepatoblasts (Figure 2F). However, we did not observe the expression of other oval cell markers, including EpCAM, AFP, and Sox9, in the colony lysates, (Figure 2E), consistent with the immunostaining data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–1H).
evidence: This is a finding from immunoblotting experiments, with reference to figures.

claim: Hepatocytes in the colonies did not exhibit oval cell-like morphology throughout the regenerative process.
source: Indeed, hepatocytes in the colonies did not exhibit oval cell-like morphology throughout the regenerative process (Figures 1A, E, 2A–C).
evidence: This is an observation from histological analysis, with reference to figures.

claim: CD133 expression in colonized hepatocytes was even higher than the embryonic liver at E17.5, which highly expressed AFP, a hepatoblast marker.
source: CD133 expression in colonized hepatocytes was even higher than the embryonic liver at E17.5, which highly expressed AFP, a hepatoblast marker (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a finding from immunoblotting experiments, with reference to a figure.

claim: The molecular size of CD133 expressed in the colonies was slightly different from that in the bile duct, likely reflecting variations in glycosylation.
source: The molecular size of CD133 expressed in the colonies was slightly different from that in the bile duct (Figure 2E), likely reflecting variations in glycosylation (Barkeer et al., 2018; Kemper et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a finding from immunoblotting experiments and its interpretation, with reference to a figure and citations.

claim: The colony-forming cells expressed a mature hepatocyte marker HNF4α at similar levels to non-colony areas.
source: Furthermore, the colony-forming cells expressed a mature hepatocyte marker HNF4α, at similar levels to non-colony areas (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a finding from immunoblotting experiments, with reference to a figure.

claim: The clustered CD133+ cells in SKO liver are not hepatoblasts or oval cells but are mature hepatocytes that acquire unique proliferation potential following PHx.
source: These results indicate that the clustered CD133+ cells in SKO liver are not hepatoblasts or oval cells but are mature hepatocytes that acquire unique proliferation potential following PHx.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the collective findings on marker expression and morphology.

claim: Vectors carrying a GFP and a sleeping beauty (SB) transposon were transfected into the liver by hydrodynamic tail vein injection (HTVi) to label a few hepatocytes with GFP in a mosaic pattern.
source: To determine the origin of these colonized hepatocytes by clonal tracing, we transfected vectors carrying a GFP and a sleeping beauty (SB) transposon (Ivics et al., 1997) into the liver by hydrodynamic tail vein injection (HTVi) (Liu et al., 1999; Zhang et al., 1999), which labeled a few hepatocytes with GFP in a mosaic pattern (Figure 3A, B; Mikkelsen et al., 2003; Yant et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method used, with references to figures and citations.

claim: The resulting colonies in SKO livers contained both GFP+ and GFP− cells, indicating multiple origins of hepatocytes.
source: The resulting colonies in SKO livers contained both GFP+ and GFP− cells (Figure 3B), indicating multiple origins of hepatocytes.
evidence: This is a finding from clonal tracing experiments and its interpretation, with reference to a figure.

claim: When a large GFP+ cell clone was located at a colony edge, GFP− cells were not recruited, even though the surrounding hepatocytes were mostly GFP-negative.
source: When a large GFP+ cell clone was located at a colony edge, we did not see the recruitment of GFP− cells, even though the surrounding hepatocytes were mostly GFP-negative (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a finding from clonal tracing experiments, with reference to a figure.

claim: The colonies were expanded by the proliferation of cells from inside rather than by continuous recruitment of surrounding hepatocytes.
source: Thus, the colonies were expanded by the proliferation of cells from inside rather than by continuous recruitment of surrounding hepatocytes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the clonal tracing observations, with reference to a figure.

claim: Hepatocytes within the colonies divided much more actively than those located outside.
source: By measuring clone sizes of GFP+ hepatocytes inside and outside, we found that hepatocytes within the colonies divided much more actively than those located outside (Figure 3D, E), suggesting that clustering enabled hepatocytes to divide actively (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is a finding from quantitative analysis of clone sizes, with reference to figures.

claim: Clustering enabled hepatocytes to divide actively.
source: By measuring clone sizes of GFP+ hepatocytes inside and outside, we found that hepatocytes within the colonies divided much more actively than those located outside (Figure 3D, E), suggesting that clustering enabled hepatocytes to divide actively (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the clone size data, with reference to figures.

claim: The starting colony size at the fate determination stage was estimated to be approximately 10 hepatocytes, based on the GFP+ clone/colony size ratios.
source: The starting colony size at the fate determination stage (Figure 3F) was estimated to be approximately 10 hepatocytes, based on the GFP+ clone/colony size ratios (Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a calculation based on experimental data, with reference to figures.

claim: The initial colony size should be large enough to include a variety of hepatocytes, signifying that the colony-forming potential does not require a special property of hepatocytes.
source: The initial colony size should be large enough to include a variety of hepatocytes, signifying that the colony-forming potential does not require a special property of hepatocytes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the estimated colony size.

claim: The existence of mononuclear and binuclear cells in the colonies 2 days after PHx further supports their heterogeneity in origin.
source: The existence of mononuclear and binuclear cells (Duncan et al., 2010) in the colonies 2 days after PHx further supports their heterogeneity in origin (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is an observation from immunostaining and its interpretation, with reference to a figure and citation.

claim: A similar pattern of colony formation was observed in cultures of primary hepatocytes isolated from SKO liver.
source: A similar pattern of colony formation was observed in cultures of primary hepatocytes isolated from SKO liver. evidence: This is a finding from in vitro experiments, with reference to figures.

claim: Shp2-negative hepatocytes formed unique colonies of Ki67+ cells in vitro, resembling the observed clusters in liver sections.
source: A similar pattern of colony formation was observed in cultures of primary hepatocytes isolated from SKO liver. Shp2-negative hepatocytes formed unique colonies of Ki67+ cells in vitro, resembling the observed clusters in liver sections (Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), while proliferating hepatocytes were distributed rather randomly in the WT culture (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a finding from in vitro experiments, with reference to figures.

claim: Proliferating hepatocytes were distributed rather randomly in the WT culture.
source: A similar pattern of colony formation was observed in cultures of primary hepatocytes isolated from SKO liver. Shp2-negative hepatocytes formed unique colonies of Ki67+ cells in vitro, resembling the observed clusters in liver sections (Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), while proliferating hepatocytes were distributed rather randomly in the WT culture (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a finding from in vitro experiments, with reference to figures.

claim: E-cadherin expression in cell-cell contacts distinguished the colonies in primary hepatocyte culture.
source: E-cadherin expression in cell-cell contacts distinguished these colonies (Figure 3H), featuring their similar properties to those in vivo.
evidence: This is a finding from immunostaining of cultured cells, with reference to a figure.

claim: The colony phenotype in primary hepatocyte culture was independent of colony sizes and was not due to high cell density in the area.
source: This phenotype was independent of colony sizes and, therefore, was not due to high cell density in the area (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is an observation from in vitro experiments, with reference to a figure.

claim: The colony formation in primary hepatocyte culture confirms their origin from mature hepatocytes.
source: The colony formation in primary hepatocyte culture also confirms their origin from mature hepatocytes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the in vitro experiments.

claim: CCl4 is metabolized by hepatocytes around the central veins into a hyper-oxidative chemical that causes necrosis and apoptosis in the area.
source: CCl4 is metabolized by hepatocytes around the central veins into a hyper-oxidative chemical that causes necrosis and apoptosis in the area (Forbes and Newsome, 2016; Weber et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge about CCl4 toxicity, supported by citations.

claim: At 2 days after CCl4 injection, distinctive CD133+ hepatocyte clusters were detected in SKO livers with a higher proliferation rate than the surrounding areas.

claim: CCl4 induced ductular reaction by CD133+ bile duct epithelial cells, but these areas were not associated with the CD133+ hepatocyte clusters.

claim: While bile duct epithelial cells were EpCAM+, CD133+ hepatocytes did not express EpCAM in the CCl4 model.
source: Consistent with the PHx model, while bile duct epithelial cells were EpCAM+, CD133+ hepatocytes did not express EpCAM (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a finding from immunostaining experiments, with reference to a figure.

claim: The CD133+ hepatocyte colonies appeared around the injured area in the CCl4 model, consistent with the notion of midlobular hepatocytes located next to a pericentral injury site.

claim: The SKO cells scattered within DKO colonies only proliferated as much as DKO cells, arguing against a cell-autonomous role of CD133.
source: Next, we labeled SKO hepatocytes by injecting AAV-GFP into SKO mice, and mixed the GFP-labelled SKO cells with DKO hepatocytes at a 1:10 ratio in culture (Figure 8E). If CD133 had a cell-autonomous function, the SKO cells in a DKO cell pool were expected to proliferate similarly as in a pure SKO cell pool. For example, if CD133 serves as a receptor, SKO cells in the mixture should still receive a ligand signal from DKO cells. By contrast, the SKO cells scattered within DKO colonies only proliferated as much as DKO cells (Figure 8F, G), arguing against a cell-autonomous role of CD133.
evidence: This is a finding from cell mixing experiments and its interpretation, with reference to figures.

claim: CD133 expression is not strictly associated with cell identity but rather is modulated by intra- and inter-cellular signals.
source: Although CD133 was thought to label stem cells in normal and tumor tissues, its expression is not restricted to the stem cell populations in either case. We found that CD133 expression was transiently induced in Shp2- and MET-deficient hepatocytes in regenerating livers damaged by PHx or CCl4. Of note, the CD133 upregulation was not accompanied by an increase in other stem/progenitor cell markers or associated with cell lineage transition. Furthermore, the reversable CD133 induction was detected in several types of cancer cells following the suppression of RTK-Ras-Erk signaling by chemical inhibition of Shp2 or Mek. These data on dynamic CD133 expression suggest that its expression pattern is not strictly associated with cell identity but rather is modulated by intra- and inter-cellular signals, which may clarify some conflicting data and notions documented in the literature.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the collective findings on CD133 expression dynamics.

claim: The putative role of CD133 in mediating intercellular sharing of materials explains why CD133/Prom1 deletion did not affect general development in mice.
source: This study identified CD133-associated filaments that connect neighboring cells (Figure 5). Super-resolution microscopy and immuno-EM further demonstrated that CD133 was primarily located on intracellular vesicles. The CD133+ vesicles may mediate intercellular sharing of materials between tightly contacting cells with minimal diffusion. This putative role of CD133 explains why CD133/Prom1 deletion did not affect general development in mice, as CD133+ vesicles are mainly generated in stress responses.
